niche: a gas and electric utility's customer hardship fund: how many of this year's grant customers will need another grant next heating season, pledged by operating district to the fund's administrator before the season opens
answer: We should fund 60 renewal caseworkers for PY2028.

stakeholder_role: analyst in the utility's customer assistance and regulatory filings team

spine.entity: one hardship-fund grant credited to a customer's account at a service address

driver: A unit's chance of needing the service again next period is set by the cumulative history of the place it occupies, counted across every occupant, not by its own history, a count reached only by carrying a retired system's records to the place through the account conversion; the forward roster's newcomers sit unusually often at places with long histories while every count and rate on the units themselves stays ordinary, so every unit-level route underforecasts.
driver_concrete: A hardship-grant customer comes back the next programme year at about 20 per cent where the service address has carried fewer than three grants in its life and about 75 per cent where it has carried three or more, whoever received them; grants to 2024-25 sit in the legacy billing archive and reach platform premises only through the account conversion; 2026-27's first-time customers sit at long-history addresses about three times as often as any settled season's did (37.7 against 10 to 12 per cent) while the roster and every district's first-time count stay on trend, so the close-out's pooled rate and every customer-level history table understate 2027-28 renewals and the caseworkers sized from them.
stump: A solver who rebuilds each 2026-27 customer's own grant history through the account conversion and applies the customer-level renewal table (or the close-out's pooled rate) expects about 5,080 renewals and funds 51 caseworkers against 60, because half of 2026-27's grant customers, and about 38 per cent of its first-time customers, sit at addresses with three or more lifetime grants, where customers come back at 75 per cent whatever their own history.

differentiation.task37: task37 asks whether an enrolment survives its cohort's end through a linked sponsor's agreement status; this build's decisive quantity is a forward return rate set by the grant history of the address a customer lives at, counted across every tenant, with the forward roster's first-timers shifted onto long-history addresses.
differentiation.task44: task44's moderator is how a period orders an item, read off one pick log in one window; this build's moderator is the cumulative grant count of a different entity (the service address) reached through a cross-system account conversion, and it is the address's history, not the customer's, that sets next year's return.
differentiation.task46: task46's rate law lives in each unit's own cumulative service exposure rebuilt from a movement log, with a cohort crossing an exposure step forward; here no unit crosses anything, the law lives in another entity's history (the address, across tenants), and the forward error comes from newcomers placed at long-history addresses while the units' own histories are ordinary.
differentiation.task65: task65 regroups child records by their own parcel so a per-entity cap binds differently, a static aggregation for a fee; here the place is the covariate of a forward behavioural rate, not the unit a cap is applied to, and nothing is regrouped or capped.
differentiation.task66: task66 classifies each dwelling's current year-round status from supply continuity on its point of delivery, pinned by a corpus of adjudications; here nothing is classified, the decisive quantity is next year's return rate, and it is set by how many grants the address has carried across all its tenants, which only the outcome record pins.
differentiation.task83: task83 conditions a measured effect on each unit's own prior treatment history; here the unit's own history is the validated decoy and the law lives in the address's history across tenants.
